claims.text: A tungsten-based high-entropy alloy containing V, Cr, and other low-activation elements can serve as a promising structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
The proposed starting material is a tungsten-dominant W–V–Cr–X refractory HEA ingot.
Such an alloy can be prepared by arc melting or vacuum induction melting in an as-cast form.
The proposed intervention is homogenization followed by neutron or ion irradiation testing.
Representative fusion service includes high temperature of at least 800 °C, thermal loading, helium implantation, and neutron fluence.
The alloy will possess refined grain boundaries stabilized by high-entropy effects and low-activation solute additions.
Multiple principal elements reduce irradiation-defect mobility.
Reduced defect mobility mitigates irradiation damage.
Low-activation alloying limits the formation of radioactive isotopes.
The proposed alloy will have enhanced high-temperature mechanical performance compared with conventional tungsten-based alloys.
The proposed alloy will exhibit less long-lived radioactivation than conventional tungsten-based alloys.
Pure tungsten or standard tungsten alloys exhibit greater Swiss-cheese-like helium-bubble damage than the proposed alloy.
Pure tungsten or standard tungsten alloys exhibit greater long-term activation than the proposed alloy.
The alloy composition must balance high-entropy effects against solute diffusivity.
Long-duration irradiation testing is required to establish minimal activation and microstructural stability.
Long-term void swelling, helium- and hydrogen-induced damage, and mechanical stability at high fluence remain empirically uncertain.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies homogenizing the alloy before irradiation, whereas the falsification experiment specifies irradiation of an as-cast W–V–Cr–X alloy; thus the proposed test does not clearly test the stated processed material.
